name: Barn-pole paradox
seoDesc: Barn-pole paradox: work out speed (v) from the speed ratio and the length of the barn. A free physics calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: The Barn-pole paradox calculator turns the speed ratio, the length of the barn and more into speed (v). That makes it useful for a lab report, a problem set or a sanity check on a physical situation. The unit chips sit next to the boxes, which is where most hand-calculation mistakes start.

sections.title: How does the Barn-pole paradox calculator work?
sections.html:
The Barn-pole paradox calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports speed (v) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the frame of reference); then you type in the speed ratio (ß), the length of the barn (L), the contracted pole length and the back of the pole leaves (Barn frame of reference).

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Barn-pole paradox calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Speed (v)=speed ratio (ß) × speed of light in the vacuum
Lorentz parameter (γ)=(1 − (speed ratio (ß) ^ 2), -1 ÷ 2)
Lorentz parameter (γ)=length of the pole (l) ÷ contracted pole length
Speed (v)=contracted pole length ÷ (back of the pole enters − front of the pole enters)
Speed (v)=-length of the barn (L) ÷ (front of the pole enters − front of the pole leaves)
Front of the pole enters=(-length of the barn (L) − contracted pole length + back of the pole leaves × speed (v)) ÷ speed (v)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take Frame of reference set to Barn, Speed of light in the vacuum = 10 m/s and Speed ratio (ß) = 10. The calculator returns Speed (v) = 100 c.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Speed (v) = 100 c should be roughly the size you expected from Frame of reference set to Barn and Speed of light in the vacuum = 10 m/s.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Speed, opening in light speed
  • Speed, opening in meters per second
  • Length, opening in meters
  • Length, opening in meters
  • Length, opening in meters
  • Time, opening in nanoseconds
  • Time, opening in nanoseconds
  • Time, opening in nanoseconds

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Barn-pole paradox calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the speed ratio, the length of the barn and the contracted pole length — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Barn-pole paradox calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns speed (v), derived from the speed ratio, the length of the barn and the contracted pole length. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Barn-pole paradox calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the speed ratio, the length of the barn, the contracted pole length and the back of the pole leaves, which is 6 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter speed (v) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Speed (v) opens in light speed and the chip beside it offers 25 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Speed (v) = 100 c. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Barn-pole paradox calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
